title: Auto-generate Postman Collections from traffic
summary: Export recorded HTTP requests to Postman collections. Add assertions, test credentials, and variables, then review updates before running in CI.
body_markdown:
Recorded requests can save time when building a Postman collection. The export gives you requests and saved examples; review authentication, variables, target hosts, and assertions before running it as a test. The screenshots below show an earlier UI, while the commands use the current export workflow.


## 1. Install Postman and proxymock


Install[Postman](https://www.postman.com/downloads/) and follow the[proxymock installation guide](https://docs.speedscale.com/proxymock/getting-started/installation/) . For a cloud snapshot, use the[speedctl Postman export guide](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/integrations/export/postman/) .


## 2. Record traffic


With your application already running on port 8080, start the recorder:


```text
proxymock   record   --app-port   8080
```


Send representative requests through the recorder’s inbound listener, normally port 4143. Configure the application’s outbound proxy routing separately if you need dependency traffic. Stop recording with Ctrl-C after the exchanges complete. Review capture coverage and sensitive values before exporting.


## 3. Export a collection


Export the local recording to a separate file:


```text
proxymock   export   postman   --in   ./proxymock   --out   collection.json
```


Inbound traffic is selected by default. Add` --inbound-only=false` to include eligible outbound HTTP exchanges, or use` --service` and` --limit` to narrow the selection. Confirm the recording directory if you chose a custom output path.


For an existing cloud snapshot, use` speedctl export snapshot --type postman --output collection.json SNAPSHOT_ID` , replacing` SNAPSHOT_ID` with the real identifier.


## 4. Import into Postman


Use Postman’s Import action and select` collection.json` . Check the target hosts and replace captured credentials with test variables before sending requests.


## 5. Add assertions and maintain the collection


Requests are grouped by host and include saved responses. Add[post-response tests](https://learning.postman.com/docs/tests-and-scripts/write-scripts/test-scripts/) for the outcomes you expect, plus any variable extraction and request chaining. A saved response example is not an executable assertion.


When the API changes, export to a new file and review the differences. Preserve intentional tests and variables instead of overwriting the maintained collection with an unreviewed export.


## Further reading


Once traffic is recorded by Speedscale it can be used for a variety of purposes:


- local API testing (like with this blog!)
- periodic testing as part of the CI pipeline - check out our docs for Github, Gitlab, and Jenkins[integration](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/cicd/)
- automated load testing
- automatic mocking of 3rd party dependencies like AWS or Google APIs


Review the[current export options](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/integrations/export/postman/) and[contact Speedscale](https://speedscale.com/contact-us/) with workflow questions.


## Frequently asked questions


### Does exporting a collection also create assertions?


The export creates HTTP requests and saved response examples in a Postman collection. Those examples are reference data, not automatically executable assertions. Add post-response tests for status, meaningful content, and the intended business outcome. Configure variables and request chaining where needed, then prove a deliberately incorrect response makes the automated collection run fail.


### How are secrets and authentication represented?


Treat the exported file as potentially sensitive: recorded request headers and response examples can retain credential values and private data. Replace credentials with variables resolved through an appropriate secret mechanism, select test identities, and review bodies and query parameters too. Exporting or importing a collection does not refresh expired tokens or automatically make its contents safe to commit.


### How do I refresh a collection when traffic changes?


Export a new reviewed recording to a separate file, compare its requests and examples with the maintained collection, and carry forward intentional tests and variables. Check the target hosts before executing it. Inbound-only is the default; include outbound calls explicitly when needed. Re-recording updates observed exchanges, but does not establish that assertion logic or provider behavior remains correct.
